messages.subject: Standardizing observed values
messages.body_plain:
Hei,

Up to now I have been running INLA mainly with artificial datasets with more or less standardized variables. I wonder how default prior specifications in INLA work with arbitrary scale of data. Say I have some observed values (y) coming from N(100, 9) and I want to infer some model parameters, say a simple linear regression on x (y = a + bx + e). Is it ok to:
A) run INLA directly on "raw" y or
B) should I standardize y first and then transform marginals (for a and b) to match the "raw" scale of y

Thanks!

Regards, Gregor

messages.body_plain:
Tnx for the prompt reply!

I tested the behaviour using the example bellow. It seems that I get more or less the same results if I standardize y or not even for N(100, 3), which is quite of from "normal", i.e. N(0, 1). I have been running some models with fixed variances and I got trapped by my own mistake of not scaling that parameter two, which lead me to the initial question. Bellow is an example that shows what I have been fiddling with.

N.B. recently submitted summary.inla.marginal returns NA for SD, because inla.emarginal still does not work for vectors.

gg

---

library(package="INLA")

n     <- 100
mu    <- 100
b     <-  1
x     <-  runif(n, min=-1, max=1) * 10
eta   <- mu + b*x
sigma <- 3
y     <- rnorm(n, mean=eta, sd=sigma)
hist(y)

data <- list(y=y, x=x)

formula <- y ~ 1 + x
result <- inla(formula, family="gaussian", data=data)
summary(result)

## Fixed effects:
##                  mean         sd 0.025quant  0.5quant 0.975quant          kld
## (Intercept) 99.706086 0.33902820 99.0393748 99.706071 100.372013 3.697785e-32
## x            1.016441 0.06000464  0.8984381  1.016439   1.134303 0.000000e+00
## Model hyperparameters:
##                                         mean    sd      0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant
## Precision for the Gaussian observations 0.09119 0.01272 0.06840    0.09048  0.11827

data$yS <- (data$y - mu ) / sigma
formulaS <- yS ~ 1 + x
resultS <- inla(formulaS, family="gaussian", data=data)
summary(resultS)

## Fixed effects:
##                    mean         sd 0.025quant    0.5quant 0.975quant kld
## (Intercept) -0.09796953 0.11303802 -0.3202645 -0.09797383  0.1240614   0
## x            0.33881461 0.02000649  0.2994707  0.33881394  0.3781117   0
## Model hyperparameters:
##                                         mean   sd     0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant
## Precision for the Gaussian observations 0.8200 0.1146 0.6155     0.8132   1.0649

marginal.mu <http://marginal.mu> <- inla.tmarginal(fun=function(x) (x * sigma) + mu, marginal=resultS$marginals.fixed$'(Intercept)')
marginal.b  <- inla.tmarginal(fun=function(x) (x * sigma),      marginal=resultS$marginals.fixed$x)

inla.marginal.summary <- function(x, ...)
{
  ## x - marginal as defined in ?inla.emarginal
  ## ... - other arguments
  m1 <- inla.emarginal(fun=function(z) z,   marginal=x, ...)
  m2 <- inla.emarginal(fun=function(z) z^2, marginal=x, ...)
  s  <- sqrt(m2 - m1^2)
  q  <- inla.qmarginal(p=c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), marginal=x, ...)
  c(mean=m1, sd=s, "0.025quant"=q[1], "0.5quant"=q[2], "0.975quant"=q[3])
}

inla.marginal.summary(marginal.mu <http://marginal.mu>)
##       mean          sd  0.025quant    0.5quant  0.975quant
## 99.7060910   0.3391141  99.0384939  99.7040911 100.3696893
## 99.706086    0.3390282  99.0393748  99.7060710 100.3720130 from raw scale
inla.marginal.summary(marginal.b)
##       mean         sd 0.025quant   0.5quant 0.975quant
## 1.01644375 0.06001948 0.89828610 1.01609006 1.13389351
## 1.016441   0.06000464 0.8984381  1.016439   1.134303   from raw scale

## --> we get the same results if we run INLA on: A) "raw" values or B) standardized y and rescale marginals back to "raw" scale

data$yS <- (data$y - mu ) / sigma
formulaS <- yS ~ 1 + x
resultS2 <- inla(formulaS, family="gaussian", data=data, control.data=list(initial=log(1/(sigma^2)), fixed=TRUE), inla.call=inlaCall,)
summary(resultS2)
## Fixed effects:
##                   mean         sd 0.025quant    0.5quant 0.975quant kld
## (Intercept) -0.0979703 0.30569756 -0.6983138 -0.09798029  0.5015313   0
## x            0.3388138 0.05410525  0.2325593  0.33881199  0.4449192   0
## The model has no hyperparameters

marginal.mu <http://marginal.mu> <- inla.tmarginal(fun=function(x) (x * sigma) + mu, marginal=resultS2$marginals.fixed$'(Intercept)')
marginal.b  <- inla.tmarginal(fun=function(x) (x * sigma),      marginal=resultS2$marginals.fixed$x)

inla.marginal.summary(marginal.mu <http://marginal.mu>)
##        mean          sd  0.025quant    0.5quant  0.975quant
##  99.7060891   0.9170926  97.9032252  99.7006834 101.4981416
##  99.706086    0.3390282  99.0393748  99.7060710 100.3720130 from raw scale
inla.marginal.summary(marginal.b)
##       mean         sd 0.025quant   0.5quant 0.975quant
##  1.0164413  0.1623157  0.6973533  1.0154845  1.3336157
## 1.016441   0.06000464 0.8984381  1.016439   1.134303   from raw scale

## --> however, this is not the case when variances are being fixe as we need to scale variance as well

resultS3 <- inla(formulaS, family="gaussian", data=data, control.data=list(initial=log(1/((sigma/sigma)^2)), fixed=TRUE), inla.call=inlaCall,)
summary(resultS3)
## Fixed effects:
##                   mean         sd 0.025quant    0.5quant 0.975quant kld
## (Intercept) -0.0979703 0.30569756 -0.6983138 -0.09798029  0.5015313   0
## x            0.3388138 0.05410525  0.2325593  0.33881199  0.4449192   0
## The model has no hyperparameters

marginal.mu <http://marginal.mu> <- inla.tmarginal(fun=function(x) (x * sigma) + mu, marginal=resultS3$marginals.fixed$'(Intercept)')
marginal.b  <- inla.tmarginal(fun=function(x) (x * sigma),      marginal=resultS3$marginals.fixed$x)

inla.marginal.summary(marginal.mu <http://marginal.mu>)
##       mean          sd  0.025quant    0.5quant  0.975quant
## 99.7060920   0.3056998  99.1051330  99.7042901 100.3034471
## 99.706086    0.3390282  99.0393748  99.7060710 100.3720130 from raw scale
inla.marginal.summary(marginal.b)
##       mean         sd 0.025quant   0.5quant 0.975quant
## 1.01644392 0.05410571 0.91008037 1.01612499 1.12216962
## 1.016441   0.06000464 0.8984381  1.016439   1.134303   from raw scale

## --> now we are closer, but there is some underestimation of posterior standard deviation

messages.subject: Doubt about Gaussian model for stochastic volatility
messages.subject_clean: Doubt about Gaussian model for stochastic volatility
messages.body_plain:
In the Gaussian stochastic volatility model, the estimation using the log of the square of the observed variable y_t leads to a linear autoregressive state space model in the form:

log (y_t^2) =- 1.27 + h_t+ w_t
h_t = alpha + rho*h_t_1+v_t

with w_t = log (e_t^2), e_t ~ N(0.1)
E(log (e_t^2)) =- 1.27
VAR(log (e_t ^ 2)) = 4.94

then the likelihood is a log-chi-square(1). In the INLA stochvol gaussian likelihood of the stochastic volatility model is used the exact log-chi-square(1) distribution or the Gaussian approximation?

Best Regards

Márcio Laurini

Link - http://harrisd.net/papers/ARCHSV/Multivariate 20Stochastic%%% 20Volatility 20Models/JacquierPolsenRossi1994JoBES.pdf

messages.body_plain:
Håvard

Thanks again for your attention

The analysis in the article of Jaquier, Polson and Rossi uses a Monte Carlo experiment with 9 different parameter settings for analyzing the performance of the MCMC estimator with sample size 500. The nine different parameter settings give rise to three relations Var (h) / E [h] ^ 2, with values of 10, 1 and .1. The estimation it assumes diffuse priors with means for alpha =-. 5, phi =. 5 and sigmav =. 1, and same initial values in the MCMC procedure (although they do not put the exact value of the variance in the priors)
The table of results puts in the first line the value of the parameter, below the average value of the posterior means, and in the third line the RMSE. In the table are placed three parameters per line, giving the results for the nine configurations.
I've managed to improve results in comparison with the previous table, instead of using the initial values of Jaquier, Polson and Rossi I use the defaults of the INLA, and putting the  restart option in control.inla equal to 10 times. The code used is below.
But I still there are many estimations where INLA ends unexpectedly reporting a problem in the Hessian, and the results for persistence (phi) when  Var (h) / E [h] ^ 2 =. 1 are still inferior to article of Jaquier, Polson and Rossi, although in general for the other parameters the results are superior in terms of RMSE.

The new results (only using 30 replications) are:

\begin{center}

\begin{tabular}{rrrrrrrrrr}

 & alpha & phi & sigma & alpha & phi & sigma & alpha & phi & sigma \\

thetaest=array(0,dim=c(3,9,nrep))

#simulated data
exp=1

while (exp<10){

alpha=thetavector[1,exp]
phi=thetavector[2,exp]
sigmav=thetavector[3,exp]
crep=0
while(crep<nrep){
n=500
eta=rep(0.1,n)
for(i in 2:n)
eta[i]=alpha+phi*(eta[i-1]-alpha)+rnorm(1,0,sigmav)

thetaest[3,exp,crep]=sqrt(1/prec)
cat("exp ",exp," it ",crep,"alpha ",alpha, " ",thetaest[1,exp,crep]," phi ",phi," ",thetaest[2,exp,crep]," sigmav",sigmav, " ",thetaest[3,exp,crep],"\n")
}
}
exp=exp+1
}

save.image("j:/minlasv/final1/montecarlosv2.Rimage")
load("j:/minlasv/final1/montecarlosv2.Rimage")

fthetavector=thetaest

Hi!

strictly speaking, your eta[1] should be

	eta[1] = rnorm(1,0,sigmav/sqrt(1-phi^2)) + alpha

so its a sample from the stationary distribution.

you're sure there is not a ^2 missing here?

	 mprec=((sigmavp)*(1-phip^2))

as sigmavp is stddev ?????

anyway, try these options, and see if its improves for the 'wrong' ones

inla(formula,family="stochvol",data=data,
control.fixed=list(mean.intercept=alphap, prec.intercept=.01),
control.inla=list(int.strategy = "grid", strategy = "laplace",
diff.logdens=5, h=0.001))

also note that the AR1 model in inla place the prior for the *marginal*
precision and NOT the innovation precision. so, maybe you have used a
different prior for the mcmc-runs and the INLA runs ????  [see the doc
for the AR1 model ]

Best

H

messages.subject: applying the observation matrix, A, only to one of the terms in the linear predictor
messages.subject_clean: applying the observation matrix, A, only to one of the terms in the linear predictor
messages.body_plain:
Just thought I would report on a trick to do this. My reading of the documentation is that if you want the observations related to linear combinations of the linear predictor, you are forced to apply the same linear combinations to all of the additive terms in the linear predictor.  I.e., you could fit a model like Y~Poi( E * (A*X*beta + A*f)).

Instead, I wanted to fit the following model:

Y ~ Poi( E * exp( X*beta + A*f))

where Y and X are nx1 vectors, f is mx1 and A is nxm.  In my case f was a spatial effect.

Basically I extended the spatial grid for f by adding on at least n nodes (actually more than n in order to retain a rectangular grid - let q be the additional number of nodes I needed beyond n to make the grid rectangular).

n=2052
m1=99;m2=101
m2extra=21
q=m1*m2extra-n

I then created a new A:

Anew = cbind( A, diag(rep(1,n)), matrix(0,n,q))
Anew = Matrix(Anew,sparse=TRUE)

I then added 0s to X so that Anew*Xnew = X:

Xnew = c(rep(0,m),X,rep(0,q))

and I created a set of weights to zero out the effect of the extra nodes of f so that only the original nodes in f affect the response (through the original A matrix):

wgts = c(rep(1,m),rep(0,n+q))
node=1:(m+n+q)

formula= y ~ -1+x + f(node,wgts, model="rw2d", nrow=m1, ncol=m2+m2extra)
mod=inla(formula,data=list(y=y,x=Xnew,node=node,wgts=wgts),E=E,control.predictor=list(A=Anew),family='Poisson')

It's a bit of extra computation but you'll see that Anew*(beta*Xnew + fnew) = beta*X+A*f so it does what I need.

Not sure if this situation is common enough that having the functionality to specify that A should be applied to only some of the components of the linear predictor would be useful to others.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Chris!!!

You're right about your comments. We came across the same problem a
while ago and had to invent a similar solution.

We don't know how to solve this issue in general as there can be many
'f's and more complicated structure with various A's.

Our approach was similar and just a variant of the same theme, and I
include it here just in case others read this post. ( I don't think
there is any need to extend the grid, as if the index=NA then there will
be no contribution from that term; see
http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-How-does-inla-deal-with-NA-s-in-the)

If the first part of the linear predictor is  (with a slight abuse of
columna vectors...)

	eta.1  = X*beta

and the second part is

	eta.2 = f

then for

	eta = [ eta.1; eta.2 ]

we can make out data-linear-predictor, eta*, as

	eta* = [ I ; A ] [ eta.1 ; eta.2 ]

as the ``A'' matrix (here, [ I; A ] ) in the control.predictor does not
need to be square.

if anyone has suggestions to solve this in more general, please let us
know!

Best,
H
